note: Every entry carries its exact math, a primary source, and an honest caveat. The card generator rotates through entries whose 'kind' it can compute for the day's PM2.5 value. Unsourced numbers do not ship.

comparisons.phrase: Breathing {city} air today = smoking {result} cigarettes. No lighter needed.
comparisons.source_name: Berkeley Earth, Air Pollution and Cigarette Equivalence (Richard A. Muller and Elizabeth A. Muller)
comparisons.caveat: A rule of thumb comparing health effects, not identical smoke. The authors call it a rough estimate, and unlike smoking, polluted air is breathed by everyone including kids.

comparisons.phrase: A week of air like this = {result} cigarettes. Your lungs are keeping the receipts.
comparisons.source_name: Berkeley Earth, Air Pollution and Cigarette Equivalence
comparisons.caveat: Extends the Berkeley Earth per-day rule of thumb across a week at the same level. Real weeks vary day to day.

comparisons.math: packs = daily mean PM2.5 / 440, where 440 = 20 cigarettes x 22 ug/m3
comparisons.phrase: Today is {result} of a full pack of cigarettes, just from breathing.
comparisons.source_name: Berkeley Earth, Air Pollution and Cigarette Equivalence
comparisons.caveat: Derived from the Berkeley Earth rule (22 ug/m3 per cigarette, 20 per pack). Only shown on days above 220 ug/m3, where pack math stops being hyperbole.

comparisons.phrase: That is {result}x the WHO daily safe limit. The limit is 15. We are not close.
comparisons.source_name: WHO, 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines (PM2.5 24-hour average 15 ug/m3)
comparisons.caveat: WHO guidelines are health-based targets, not legal limits. India's own national standard (60 ug/m3 for 24h PM2.5) is four times looser.

comparisons.math: multiple = daily mean PM2.5 / 5 (WHO 2021 annual guideline)
comparisons.phrase: If every day were like today, you would live at {result}x the WHO annual safe level.
comparisons.source_name: WHO, 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines (PM2.5 annual average 5 ug/m3)
comparisons.caveat: Compares one day against an annual guideline, so it describes a hypothetical year of days like today, not your actual annual exposure.

comparisons.math: years lost = 0.98 x (PM2.5 - 5) / 10, for sustained exposure at this level relative to the WHO guideline
comparisons.phrase: Live with this air permanently and it prices out at about {result} years of life expectancy. That is the math, not a mood.
comparisons.source_name: AQLI methodology (Ebenstein et al. 2017), University of Chicago EPIC
comparisons.caveat: The AQLI conversion (0.98 years per 10 ug/m3) applies to sustained lifetime exposure, so this is what today's level would cost if it were your permanent normal, not the cost of one bad day.

comparisons.phrase: Reminder: Delhi residents are losing 8.2 years of life expectancy to PM2.5, per the AQLI 2025 report. The average Indian loses 3.5.
comparisons.caveat: Relative to permanent attainment of the WHO 5 ug/m3 guideline. A statistical average across the population, not a personal prediction.

comparisons.math: category lookup, US EPA PM2.5 24h breakpoints (2024 update)
comparisons.phrase: In the US, today's air would be officially rated '{result}'. Here it is called Tuesday.
comparisons.source_name: US EPA, Technical Assistance Document for the Reporting of Daily Air Quality (AirNow, 2024 breakpoints)
comparisons.caveat: US categories use the same pollutant with stricter cut points than India's AQI, which is why the same air sounds scarier in American.

comparisons.math: Indian AQI sub-index from PM2.5 24h mean, CPCB breakpoints
comparisons.phrase: Official Indian AQI: {aqi} out of 500, category '{result}'. That is the government's own scale.
comparisons.source_name: CPCB, National Air Quality Index (PM2.5 breakpoints)
comparisons.caveat: Computed from PM2.5 alone. The full CPCB AQI takes the worst sub-index across pollutants, so the official city AQI can be higher on days another pollutant dominates.

comparisons.phrase: Outdoor air pollution causes about 4.2 million early deaths a year worldwide, says WHO. It is one of the biggest killers nobody posts about.
comparisons.source_name: WHO fact sheet, Ambient (outdoor) air quality and health (2019 estimate)
comparisons.caveat: A modeled global estimate for 2019, the latest WHO headline figure, with uncertainty in the millions.

comparisons.phrase: Plot twist: 68 percent of outdoor air pollution deaths are heart disease and stroke. It was never just about your lungs.
comparisons.source_name: WHO fact sheet, Ambient (outdoor) air quality and health
comparisons.caveat: WHO's breakdown of premature deaths linked to outdoor air pollution: 68 percent ischaemic heart disease and stroke, 14 percent COPD, 14 percent acute lower respiratory infection, 4 percent lung cancer.

comparisons.phrase: The most polluted city on Earth in the 2025 IQAir report is Loni, in Delhi NCR: 112.5 ug/m3 average, 22x the WHO limit. All 25 worst cities were in India, Pakistan and China.
comparisons.source_name: IQAir, 2025 World Air Quality Report press release
comparisons.caveat: IQAir rankings blend government and low-cost sensor data and only cover cities that measure at all. Plenty of unmonitored places never make the list.

comparisons.phrase: A NIOSH N95 removes at least 95 percent of airborne particles when it seals to your face. On days like this, it is not paranoia, it is arithmetic.
comparisons.source_name: CDC NIOSH, Proper N95 Respirator Use (Science Bulletin)
comparisons.caveat: The 95 percent is the certified filter performance with a proper seal. Beards, gaps and surgical masks do not deliver it.

comparisons.phrase: Kids breathe faster than adults, so they absorb more of this per kilo. They also live closer to the ground, where some pollutants peak. WHO's words, not ours.
comparisons.source_name: WHO, More than 90% of the world's children breathe toxic air every day (2018)
comparisons.caveat: Direct WHO statements: children 'breathe more rapidly than adults and so absorb more pollutants' and 'live closer to the ground, where some pollutants reach peak concentrations'.

comparisons.math: max observed daily mean PM2.5 in this repo's archive over the current season window
comparisons.phrase: Worst day this season so far: {result} ug/m3 on {result_date}. Today is {relation} that. Receipts in the repo.
comparisons.caveat: Computed from this project's own logged observations, which start when the project started. Git history is the proof.

comparisons.math: percentile rank of today's value among this season's observed days
comparisons.phrase: Today's air is worse than {result} percent of days this season in {city}. Ranked, logged, versioned.
comparisons.caveat: Season means the trailing 90 days of this project's own observations. Small archive early on means noisy percentiles, and the repo shows exactly how small.

comparisons.math: ratio of this city's value to the cleanest tracked city today
comparisons.phrase: {city} today is {result}x the air of {other_city}, the cleanest city we track. Same country, different lungs.
comparisons.caveat: Same-day comparison across the five tracked cities using the same measurement rule for each. Only shown when the ratio is at least 1.5.
